claim: Environmental DNA from archived leaf material can characterize plant-associated arthropod communities.
source: Here, we demonstrate the utility of environmental DNA from archived leaf material to characterize plant-associated arthropod communities.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental work described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study analyzed several multi-decadal leaf time series from tree canopies in four land use types sampled as part of a long-term environmental monitoring program across Germany.
source: We base our work on several multi-decadal leaf time series from tree canopies in four land use types, which were sampled as part of a long-term environmental monitoring program across Germany.
evidence: The abstract describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: The study analyzed temporal changes in communities of several thousand arthropod species belonging to 23 orders using metabarcoding and quantitative PCR.
source: Using these highly standardized and well-preserved samples, we analyze temporal changes in communities of several thousand arthropod species belonging to 23 orders using metabarcoding and quantitative PCR.
evidence: The abstract describes the analytical methods and scope of the study.

claim: The data do not support widespread declines of α-diversity within sites.
source: Our data do not support widespread declines of α-diversity or genetic variation within sites.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the analysis.

claim: The data do not support widespread declines of genetic variation within sites.
source: Our data do not support widespread declines of α-diversity or genetic variation within sites.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the analysis.

claim: There is a gradual community turnover across all land use types and all arthropod orders.
source: Instead, we find a gradual community turnover, which results in temporal and spatial biotic homogenization, across all land use types and all arthropod orders.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the analysis.

claim: Community turnover results in temporal biotic homogenization across all land use types and all arthropod orders.
source: Instead, we find a gradual community turnover, which results in temporal and spatial biotic homogenization, across all land use types and all arthropod orders.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the analysis.

claim: Community turnover results in spatial biotic homogenization across all land use types and all arthropod orders.
source: Instead, we find a gradual community turnover, which results in temporal and spatial biotic homogenization, across all land use types and all arthropod orders.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the analysis.

claim: Insect decline is more complex than mere α-diversity loss and can be driven by β-diversity decay across space and time.
source: Our results suggest that insect decline is more complex than mere α-diversity loss, but can be driven by β-diversity decay across space and time.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Dramatic declines of terrestrial insects have been reported in recent years, particularly in areas of intensified land use.
source: Dramatic declines of terrestrial insects have been reported in recent years, particularly in areas of intensified land use (Hallmann et al., 2017; van Klink et al., 2020; Seibold et al., 2019; Sánchez-Bayo and Wyckhuys, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies reporting insect declines.

claim: Some authors have urged caution in generalizing insect decline results.
source: However, some authors have urged caution in generalizing these results (Didham et al., 2020; Thomas et al., 2019; Cardoso et al., 2019), suggesting that reported patterns of decline may be more localized than currently assumed or reflect long-term natural abundance fluctuations (Macgregor et al., 2019; Crossley et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites studies that question the generalizability of insect decline reports.

claim: Most studies on insect decline suffer from a lack of long-term time series data.
source: Most studies on insect decline suffer from a lack of long-term time series data and are limited in geographic and taxonomic breadth, often using biomass as a proxy for diversity estimates (Hallmann et al., 2017; Daskalova et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites studies to support this limitation of existing research.

claim: Most studies on insect decline are limited in geographic and taxonomic breadth.
source: Most studies on insect decline suffer from a lack of long-term time series data and are limited in geographic and taxonomic breadth, often using biomass as a proxy for diversity estimates (Hallmann et al., 2017; Daskalova et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites studies to support this limitation of existing research.

claim: Most studies on insect decline often use biomass as a proxy for diversity estimates.
source: Most studies on insect decline suffer from a lack of long-term time series data and are limited in geographic and taxonomic breadth, often using biomass as a proxy for diversity estimates (Hallmann et al., 2017; Daskalova et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites studies to support this methodological limitation.

claim: Environmental DNA metabarcoding has offered a promising new approach to monitor biological communities.
source: In recent years, environmental DNA metabarcoding has offered a promising new approach to monitor biological communities (Taberlet et al., 2018; Tautz et al., 2002; Thomsen and Sigsgaard, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting the utility of eDNA metabarcoding.

claim: Terrestrial arthropod eDNA can be recovered from plant material.
source: This includes terrestrial arthropods, whose eDNA can be recovered from various substrates, for example plant material (Nakamura et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a study demonstrating this capability.

claim: The study analyzed 30-year time series data of arthropod communities from canopy leaf material of four tree species from 24 sites across Germany.
source: We then analyze 30-year time series data of arthropod communities from canopy leaf material of four tree species from 24 sites across Germany.
evidence: The introduction describes the scope of the dataset analyzed.

claim: The sampling sites represent four land use types with different degrees of anthropogenic disturbance: urban parks, agricultural areas, timber forests, and national parks.
source: These sites represent four land use types with different degrees of anthropogenic disturbance: urban parks, agricultural areas, timber forests, and national parks (Figure 1).
evidence: The introduction describes the land use types and references Figure 1.

claim: The samples were collected using a highly standardized protocol by the German Environmental Specimen Bank.
source: The samples were collected using a highly standardized protocol by the German Environmental Specimen Bank (ESB), a large biomonitoring effort for Germany's ecosystems, and stored at below −150°C.
evidence: The introduction describes the sample collection and storage methodology.

claim: The samples were stored at below −150°C.
source: The samples were collected using a highly standardized protocol by the German Environmental Specimen Bank (ESB), a large biomonitoring effort for Germany's ecosystems, and stored at below −150°C.
evidence: The introduction describes the sample storage conditions.

claim: Current studies on insect decline primarily focus on site-based assessments of α-diversity and biomass.
source: Current studies on insect decline primarily focus on site-based assessments of α-diversity and biomass (Hallmann et al., 2017; Seibold et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites studies to characterize the current focus of insect decline research.

claim: α-diversity and biomass metrics alone are insufficient for characterizing ongoing biodiversity change.
source: Yet, these metrics alone are insufficient for characterizing ongoing biodiversity change (Marta et al., 2021; Kortz and Magurran, 2019; Magurran and Henderson, 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting this limitation of current metrics.

claim: Significant temporal community change and declines can occur at the scale of β- or γ-diversity without affecting local richness.
source: Significant temporal community change and declines can also occur at the scale of β- or γ-diversity, without affecting local richness.
evidence: The introduction presents this as established knowledge about biodiversity change.

claim: Community change may be driven by community turnover and spatial biotic homogenization.
source: This may be driven by community turnover and spatial biotic homogenization (Karp et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites a study supporting this mechanism of biodiversity change.

claim: Fluctuating occurrences of transient species considerably increase diversity within single sites over time.
source: Fluctuating occurrences of transient species considerably increase diversity within single sites over time (D'Souza and Hebert, 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study supporting this pattern of temporal diversity variation.

claim: The loss of transient species in favor of taxa with temporally stable occurrence results in an increasingly predictable community and temporal diversity decline.
source: The loss of such transient species in favor of taxa with a temporally stable occurrence results in an increasingly predictable community and hence a temporal diversity decline.
evidence: The introduction presents this as a logical consequence of species turnover patterns.

claim: Biotic turnover may occur gradually following changing environmental conditions.
source: Biotic turnover may occur gradually following changing environmental conditions, but can also occur abruptly, when ecosystems reach tipping points (Barnosky et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites a study discussing patterns of biotic turnover.

claim: Biotic turnover can occur abruptly when ecosystems reach tipping points.
source: Biotic turnover may occur gradually following changing environmental conditions, but can also occur abruptly, when ecosystems reach tipping points (Barnosky et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites a study discussing ecosystem tipping points.

claim: The study recovered 2054 OTUs from the samples.
source: We recovered 2054 OTUs from our samples, with different tree species having significantly different OTU numbers on average (Figure 2A, linear mixed model [LMM], p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports the number of OTUs recovered and references Figure 2A.

claim: Different tree species have significantly different OTU numbers on average.
source: We recovered 2054 OTUs from our samples, with different tree species having significantly different OTU numbers on average (Figure 2A, linear mixed model [LMM], p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing differences in OTU numbers among tree species.

claim: All tree species showed a balanced and relatively similar taxonomic composition at the order level.
source: Nevertheless, all tree species showed a balanced and relatively similar taxonomic composition at the order level (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: The results section describes the taxonomic composition and references figures.

claim: The study identified 23 orders, 218 families, and 413 genera.
source: We identified 23 orders, 218 families, and 413 genera.
evidence: The results section reports the taxonomic diversity recovered.

claim: Diptera was the richest order with 600 OTUs in 48 families.
source: The richest order was Diptera (600 OTUs in 48 families), followed by Hymenoptera (369 OTUs in 21 families), Acari (293 OTUs in 21 families), Lepidoptera (233 OTUs in 32 families), Hemiptera (152 OTUs in 19 families), Coleoptera (133 OTUs in 29 families), and Araneae (99 OTUs in 15 families).
evidence: The results section reports the richness of different arthropod orders.

claim: Each tree species harbored a unique arthropod community.
source: Each tree species harbored a unique arthropod community (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, D), with typical monophagous taxa exclusively recovered from their respective host trees.
evidence: The results section describes the uniqueness of arthropod communities and references figures.

claim: Typical monophagous taxa were exclusively recovered from their respective host trees.
source: Each tree species harbored a unique arthropod community (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, D), with typical monophagous taxa exclusively recovered from their respective host trees.
evidence: The results section describes the host specificity of certain taxa.

claim: The arthropod communities from different sites and land use types were differentiated within tree species.
source: The arthropod communities from different sites and land use types were also differentiated within tree species (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, PERMANOVA, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing community differentiation and references a figure.

claim: Abundances of the spruce gall midge Piceacecis abietiperda and its parasitoid, the chalcid wasp Torymus sp., were well correlated across all analyzed spruce sites.
source: For example, abundances of the spruce gall midge Piceacecis abietiperda and its parasitoid, the chalcid wasp Torymus sp., were well correlated across all analyzed spruce sites (LM, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing correlation between host and parasitoid abundances.

claim: Piceacecis abietiperda and Torymus sp. underwent coupled abundance cycles with similar maxima every 6–8 years.
source: Both underwent coupled abundance cycles, with similar maxima every 6–8 years (Figure 2C).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal pattern of abundance cycles and references Figure 2C.

claim: The recovered community composition from ESB leaf homogenate samples was similar to hand-collected branch clipping samples.
source: The recovered community composition from ESB leaf homogenate samples was similar to hand-collected branch clipping samples (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The results section compares the two sampling methods and references figures.

claim: Branch clipping recovered a larger diversity of spiders, a taxon which is exclusively found on leaf surfaces.
source: Branch clipping recovered a larger diversity of spiders, a taxon which is exclusively found on leaf surfaces.
evidence: The results section compares the recovery of spiders between methods.

claim: About 25% of the recovered taxa from ESB leaf powder likely inhabited the insides of leaves.
source: In contrast, about 25% of the recovered taxa from ESB leaf powder likely inhabited the insides of leaves, e.g., gallers and miners (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of taxa from inside leaves and references a figure.

claim: Arthropod DNA in leaf homogenates is temporally very stable.
source: Overall, arthropod DNA in leaf homogenates appears temporally very stable: Even freeze-dried leaf material that had been stored at room temperature for 8 years yielded surprisingly similar arthropod communities to ESB samples (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The results section describes the stability of arthropod DNA in stored samples and references figures.

claim: Freeze-dried leaf material stored at room temperature for 8 years yielded surprisingly similar arthropod communities to ESB samples.
source: Overall, arthropod DNA in leaf homogenates appears temporally very stable: Even freeze-dried leaf material that had been stored at room temperature for 8 years yielded surprisingly similar arthropod communities to ESB samples (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The results section compares arthropod communities from differently stored samples and references figures.

claim: The qPCR assay accurately predicted changes in relative copy number of arthropod DNA on plant material across a 10,000-fold dilution series.
source: The qPCR assay accurately predicted changes in relative copy number of arthropod DNA on plant material across a 10,000-fold dilution series.
evidence: The results section describes the validation of the qPCR assay.

claim: Very similar CT values were recovered when comparing taxonomically heterogeneous mock communities.
source: Even when comparing taxonomically heterogeneous mock communities, very similar CT values were recovered (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), highlighting the accuracy and wide applicability of our approach.
evidence: The results section describes the validation of the qPCR assay with mock communities and references figures.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation of OTU richness and relative arthropod copy number in the ESB samples.
source: Overall, we found a significant positive correlation of OTU richness and relative arthropod copy number in the ESB samples (LMM, p < 0.05; see Methods: 'Statistical analysis'), supporting recent work suggesting a biomass–diversity relationship (Hallmann et al., 2021).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing correlation between richness and copy number.

claim: The statistical analysis does not support previously reported widespread temporal α-diversity declines.
source: Our statistical analysis does not support previously reported widespread temporal α-diversity declines (Figure 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5H, I, LMM, p > 0.05), even when different land use types are analyzed separately (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, LMM, p > 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing no significant temporal decline in α-diversity and references figures.

claim: Warm summers were negatively associated with richness.
source: Instead, warm summers and cold winters were negatively associated with richness (LMM, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing the effect of temperature on richness.

claim: Cold winters were negatively associated with richness.
source: Instead, warm summers and cold winters were negatively associated with richness (LMM, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing the effect of temperature on richness.

claim: The temporal pattern of diversity was largely independent of taxonomy.
source: The temporal pattern of diversity was also largely independent of taxonomy: most orders did not show temporal trends when analyzed separately (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal patterns across different taxonomic groups and references figures.

claim: There was a significant loss of lepidopteran diversity, primarily driven by OTU loss at urban sites.
source: Exceptions include a significant loss of lepidopteran diversity, which is primarily driven by OTU loss at urban sites, and an overall increasing diversity of mites (LMM, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing lepidopteran diversity loss at urban sites.

claim: There was an overall increasing diversity of mites.
source: Exceptions include a significant loss of lepidopteran diversity, which is primarily driven by OTU loss at urban sites, and an overall increasing diversity of mites (LMM, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing increasing mite diversity.

claim: A diversity decline across all orders was observed at only a single site.
source: The overall temporally stable diversity is also visible at separate sites; a diversity decline across all orders was observed at only a single site (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section describes site-specific diversity patterns and references a figure.

claim: Community-level zOTU richness was well correlated to OTU richness (R2 = 0.89).
source: Neither community-level zero radius OTU (zOTU) richness (which was well correlated to OTU richness, R2 = 0.89) nor within-OTU haplotype richness declined significantly over time (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The results section reports the correlation between zOTU and OTU richness.

claim: Community-level zOTU richness did not decline significantly over time.
source: Neither community-level zero radius OTU (zOTU) richness (which was well correlated to OTU richness, R2 = 0.89) nor within-OTU haplotype richness declined significantly over time (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing no significant temporal decline in zOTU richness and references figures.

claim: Within-OTU haplotype richness did not decline significantly over time.
source: Neither community-level zero radius OTU (zOTU) richness (which was well correlated to OTU richness, R2 = 0.89) nor within-OTU haplotype richness declined significantly over time (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing no significant temporal decline in haplotype richness and references figures.

claim: Relative copy number showed an overall decrease over time.
source: In contrast to the stable α-diversity, relative copy number showed an overall decrease over time (Figure 4D, LMM, p < 0.05), suggesting that arthropod biomass may indeed be declining in woodlands (Seibold et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing temporal decline in relative copy number and references a figure.

claim: The decrease in relative copy number suggests that arthropod biomass may be declining in woodlands.
source: In contrast to the stable α-diversity, relative copy number showed an overall decrease over time (Figure 4D, LMM, p < 0.05), suggesting that arthropod biomass may indeed be declining in woodlands (Seibold et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section interprets the copy number decline as potential biomass decline and cites a relevant study.

claim: The effect of copy number decrease appears to be particularly driven by urban sites.
source: The effect appears to be particularly driven by urban sites, coinciding with a loss of lepidopteran diversity (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The results section describes the land use type showing the strongest effect and references figures.

claim: Declines of arthropod DNA copy number are visible in several agricultural and timber forest sites, particularly in the last 10 years of the time series.
source: However, declines of arthropod DNA copy number are also visible in several agricultural and timber forest sites, particularly in the last 10 years of our time series (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section describes temporal patterns of copy number decline in different land use types and references figures.

claim: There was no significant difference between the average number of declining (6.94%) and increasing (10.04%) OTUs.
source: However, we found no significant difference between the average number of declining (6.94%) and increasing (10.04%) OTUs (t-test, p > 0.05, Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis comparing declining and increasing OTUs and references a figure.

claim: With the exception of Acari, declines and increases in OTU read abundance were independent of arthropod order and land use type.
source: With the exception of Acari, which showed an overrepresentation of increasing OTUs, declines and increases in OTU read abundance were independent of arthropod order and land use type (Figure 5A, B, Fisher's exact test p > 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing independence of abundance changes from taxonomy and land use, and references figures.

claim: Acari showed an overrepresentation of increasing OTUs.
source: With the exception of Acari, which showed an overrepresentation of increasing OTUs, declines and increases in OTU read abundance were independent of arthropod order and land use type (Figure 5A, B, Fisher's exact test p > 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing an exception to the general pattern for Acari.

claim: The observed replacement of about 15% of OTUs within sites translates into a significant temporal change of taxonomic β-diversity.
source: The observed replacement of about 15% of OTUs within sites translates into a significant temporal change of taxonomic β-diversity (Figure 5C, Figure 2—figure supplement 5J and K).
evidence: The results section describes the relationship between OTU replacement and β-diversity change and references figures.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation of temporal distance and Jaccard dissimilarity for most sites.
source: We found a strong positive correlation of temporal distance and Jaccard dissimilarity for most sites (PERMANOVA, p < 0.05).
evidence: The results section reports statistical analysis showing correlation between temporal distance and community dissimilarity.

claim: Species are continuously replaced in all land use types.
source: Thus, species are continuously replaced in all land use types (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section describes the pattern of species replacement and references a figure.

claim: In the majority of analyzed sites, β-diversity did not show a correlation with differences in copy number.
source: In the majority of analyzed sites, β-diversity did not show a correlation with differences in copy number (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section reports the lack of correlation between β-diversity and copy number changes and references a figure.

claim: β-Diversity between consecutive sampling years dropped significantly in many sites, particularly in beech forests.
source: The first noteworthy pattern concerns a loss of temporal β-diversity within sites. β-Diversity between consecutive sampling years dropped significantly in many sites, particularly in beech forests (Figure 5D).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal pattern of β-diversity within sites and references a figure.

claim: Diversity within sites is increasingly homogenized over time.
source: Thus, diversity within sites is increasingly homogenized over time.
evidence: The results section interprets the loss of temporal β-diversity as homogenization.

claim: There was a significant decrease of β-diversity between sites for beech forests.
source: We also found a significant decrease of β-diversity between sites for beech forests (Figure 5E).
evidence: The results section reports the temporal pattern of β-diversity between sites and references a figure.

claim: The data suggest a loss of site-specific species and a gain of more widespread generalists, irrespective of land use.
source: Our data suggest a loss of site-specific species and a gain of more widespread generalists, irrespective of land use.
evidence: The results section interprets the β-diversity patterns as species replacement.

claim: Several novel colonizers spread rapidly in woodlands and showed similar abundance trends across various sites in parallel.
source: This pattern also emerges at the level of individual OTUs. Several novel colonizers spread rapidly in woodlands and showed similar abundance trends across various sites in parallel (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes the spread of novel colonizers and references a figure.

claim: In the past decades, temporal turnover has led to temporally more predictable communities within sites.
source: In the past decades, this turnover has led to temporally more predictable communities within sites and increasingly similar communities between the two national parks.
evidence: The results section interprets the temporal turnover patterns observed in the NMDS plot.

claim: In the past decades, temporal turnover has led to increasingly similar communities between the two national parks.
source: In the past decades, this turnover has led to temporally more predictable communities within sites and increasingly similar communities between the two national parks.
evidence: The results section interprets the temporal turnover patterns observed in the NMDS plot.

claim: DNA from archived leaf material provides a robust source of data to reconstruct temporal community change across the arthropod tree of life.
source: Here, we show that DNA from archived leaf material provides a robust source of data to reconstruct temporal community change across the arthropod tree of life.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the main methodological finding of the study.

claim: Leaf samples should cover a broad phenological window because adults of many insect species are only active during a short time period of the year, but their larvae spend the whole year on their host plant.
source: Leaf samples should also cover a broad phenological window: Adults of many insect species are only active during a short time period of the year, but their larvae spend the whole year on their host plant (Gagné and Graney, 2014).
evidence: The discussion explains the advantage of leaf sampling and cites a relevant study.

claim: A Malaise trap will miss taxa whose adults are only active for a short time period most times of the year, while an eDNA approach should detect the larvae throughout.
source: A Malaise trap will miss these taxa most times of the year, while an eDNA approach should detect the larvae throughout.
evidence: The discussion compares the phenological coverage of different sampling methods.

claim: As sampled leaves make up the habitat and often food source of arthropods, it is possible to infer the exposure of arthropod communities to chemical pollution by analyzing chemicals in the leaf material.
source: As sampled leaves make up the habitat and often food source of arthropods, it is also possible to infer the exposure of arthropod communities to chemical pollution by analyzing chemicals in the leaf material.
evidence: The discussion explains an additional advantage of leaf sampling for understanding arthropod exposure to pollutants.

claim: Pesticide use has often been invoked as a driver of insect decline.
source: This is of critical importance, as pesticide use has often been invoked as a driver of insect decline (Goulson et al., 2015; Siviter et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion cites studies linking pesticides to insect decline.

claim: The high temporal stability of arthropod DNA in 8-year-old dried leaf samples suggests the utility of other plant archives, for example, herbaria, for arthropod eDNA.
source: The high temporal stability of arthropod DNA in 8-year-old dried leaf samples also suggests the utility of other plant archives, for example, herbaria, for arthropod eDNA.
evidence: The discussion extrapolates from the study findings to suggest broader applications.

claim: For less standardized and less well-preserved sample types, careful evaluation of cross-contamination or chemical DNA modification may be warranted.
source: However, for such less standardized and less well-preserved sample types, careful evaluation of cross-contamination or chemical DNA modification (Orlando et al., 2021), which could inflate the recovered diversity, may be warranted.
evidence: The discussion cautions about potential issues with less controlled samples and cites a relevant study.

claim: The study provides unprecedented insights into arthropod community change in the tree canopy, an ecosystem known for its high and often cryptic diversity.
source: We here analyze a unique leaf archive and provide unprecedented insights into arthropod community change in the tree canopy, an ecosystem known for its high and often cryptic diversity (Nakamura et al., 2017).
evidence: The discussion characterizes the significance of the study and cites a relevant study about canopy diversity.

claim: The results do not confirm the hypothesis of widespread losses of α-diversity.
source: Our results do not confirm the hypothesis of widespread losses of α-diversity.
evidence: The discussion summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Initial reports of insect declines originate mainly from grassland ecosystems that have undergone massive changes in land use.
source: Initial reports of insect declines originate mainly from grassland ecosystems that have undergone massive changes in land use (Hallmann et al., 2017).
evidence: The discussion cites a study to contextualize the difference between previous findings and the current study.

claim: Central European canopy communities may be less affected by land use change than grassland ecosystems.
source: Central European canopy communities may be less affected by such change.
evidence: The discussion speculates about why the current study did not find widespread α-diversity declines.

claim: The only sites that showed declines of richness were agricultural and urban sites.
source: Interestingly, the only sites that showed declines of richness were agricultural and urban sites, suggesting that land use may at least locally affect neighboring canopy communities (Hallmann et al., 2014).
evidence: The discussion describes site-specific patterns and cites a relevant study.

claim: Land use may at least locally affect neighboring canopy communities.
source: Interestingly, the only sites that showed declines of richness were agricultural and urban sites, suggesting that land use may at least locally affect neighboring canopy communities (Hallmann et al., 2014).
evidence: The discussion interprets the site-specific patterns and cites a relevant study.

claim: The data suggest negative effects of warm summers on richness.
source: Our data also suggest negative effects of warm summers on richness.
evidence: The discussion summarizes a finding about climate effects on richness.

claim: Climate warming has recently been suggested to act in conjunction with land use change to drive insect declines.
source: Climate warming has recently been suggested to act in conjunction with land use change to drive insect declines (Outhwaite et al., 2022).
evidence: The discussion cites a recent study about climate and land use interactions.

claim: The study detected DNA copy number declines in all land use types, suggesting that overall biomass may be in decline.
source: Instead of declining richness, we detected DNA copy number declines in all land use types, suggesting that overall biomass may indeed be in decline.
evidence: The discussion interprets the copy number findings as potential biomass decline.

claim: Extinction is the endpoint of a long trajectory of decline and increasingly affects common species.
source: Extinction is the endpoint of a long trajectory of decline and increasingly affects common species (Collen et al., 2011), hence biomass decline could foreshadow future biodiversity loss.
evidence: The discussion cites a study to support the interpretation of biomass decline as a precursor to biodiversity loss.

claim: Biomass decline could foreshadow future biodiversity loss.
source: Extinction is the endpoint of a long trajectory of decline and increasingly affects common species (Collen et al., 2011), hence biomass decline could foreshadow future biodiversity loss.
evidence: The discussion speculates about the implications of biomass decline.

claim: The dropping copy number may reflect a taxonomic turnover of species with either different eDNA shedding rates or different rDNA copy numbers in the different communities.
source: Alternatively, the dropping copy number may reflect a taxonomic turnover of species with either different eDNA shedding rates or different rDNA copy numbers in the different communities.
evidence: The discussion presents an alternative explanation for the copy number decline.

claim: If taxonomic turnover were responsible for copy number changes, an association of copy number changes and turnover would be expected, which was not found in the data.
source: However, if the latter were true, an association of copy number changes and turnover would be expected, which we did not find in our data.
evidence: The discussion evaluates the alternative explanation against the data.

claim: The study found pronounced taxonomic turnover in nearly all communities.
source: Instead of widespread losses of α-diversity, we indeed found pronounced taxonomic turnover in nearly all communities (Dornelas et al., 2014), supporting our second hypothesis.
evidence: The discussion summarizes a key finding and cites a relevant study.

claim: While resident species are continuously lost, they are mostly replaced by novel colonizers.
source: While resident species are continuously lost, they are mostly replaced by novel colonizers.
evidence: The discussion describes the pattern of species turnover.

claim: Turnover can result in biotic homogenization across space and time.
source: This turnover can result in biotic homogenization across space and time.
evidence: The discussion explains the consequence of species turnover.

claim: Less interannual variation of the occurrence of taxa within sites causes a decline in overall β-diversity.
source: Less interannual variation of the occurrence of taxa within sites and reduced spatial variation of their occurrence between sites both cause a decline in overall β-diversity.
evidence: The discussion explains the mechanisms of β-diversity decline.

claim: Reduced spatial variation of taxon occurrence between sites causes a decline in overall β-diversity.
source: Less interannual variation of the occurrence of taxa within sites and reduced spatial variation of their occurrence between sites both cause a decline in overall β-diversity.
evidence: The discussion explains the mechanisms of β-diversity decline.

claim: Biotic homogenization is often associated with intensification of land use and landscape simplification.
source: Biotic homogenization is often associated with intensification of land use (Karp et al., 2012; Gossner et al., 2016) and landscape simplification (Holland et al., 2005).
evidence: The discussion cites studies linking homogenization to land use changes.

claim: The pattern of biotic homogenization observed in the study affected all land use types equally.
source: However, the pattern we observed affected all land use types equally.
evidence: The discussion describes the universality of the homogenization pattern.

claim: The universality of the homogenization changes suggests that neither site- nor taxon-specific factors are responsible.
source: The universality of these changes suggests that neither site- nor taxon-specific factors are responsible.
evidence: The discussion infers from the universal pattern that local factors are not responsible.

claim: Possible explanations for universal homogenization include factors that act at a larger scale, such as climate change-induced range shifts, nitrogen deposition, and the introduction of invasive species.
source: Possible explanations include factors that act at a larger scale, such as climate change-induced range shifts (Marta et al., 2021), nitrogen deposition (Gámez-Virués et al., 2015), and the introduction of invasive species (Soroye et al., 2020; Lister and Garcia, 2018).
evidence: The discussion speculates about large-scale drivers and cites relevant studies.

claim: The alternative explanation that the observed community-wide turnover pattern may have resulted from shifting phenologies is unlikely given that leaf samples recover a fairly broad phenological window.
source: Given that our leaf samples recover a fairly broad phenological window, the alternative explanation that the observed community-wide turnover pattern may have resulted from shifting phenologies (Cohen et al., 2018) is unlikely.
evidence: The discussion evaluates and dismisses an alternative explanation based on the study design and cites a relevant study.

claim: The gradual replacement of species suggests that ecosystems are not yet reaching tipping points.
source: The gradual replacement of species also suggests that we are not yet observing ecosystems reaching tipping points (Barnosky et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion interprets the gradual nature of turnover and cites a relevant study.

claim: The work shows the great importance of standardized time series data to accurately reveal biodiversity change in the Anthropocene across space and time.
source: In summary, our work shows the great importance of standardized time series data to accurately reveal biodiversity change in the Anthropocene (Thomsen et al., 2016) across space and time, beyond the decline of α-diversity and biomass (Dornelas et al., 2014).
evidence: The discussion summarizes the methodological contribution and cites relevant studies.

claim: Taxonomic replacement and biotic homogenization, even in seemingly pristine habitats such as national parks, signify an important and hitherto insufficiently recognized facet of the current insect crisis.
source: Taxonomic replacement and biotic homogenization, even in seemingly pristine habitats such as national parks, signify an important and hitherto insufficiently recognized facet of the current insect crisis.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: A total of 312 leaf samples of four common German tree species were used in the study.
source: We used a total of 312 leaf samples of four common German tree species: the European Beech Fagus sylvatica (98 samples), the Lombardy Poplar Populus nigra 'italica' (65 samples), the Norway Spruce Picea abies (123 samples), and the Scots Pine Pinus sylvestris (26 samples).
evidence: The methods section describes the sample composition.

claim: The samples have been collected annually or biannually by the German Environmental Specimen Bank since the 1980s.
source: The samples have been collected annually or biannually by the German Environmental Specimen Bank (ESB) since the 1980s and serve as indicators for aerial pollutants (Schulze et al., 2007).
evidence: The methods section describes the sampling history and cites a relevant study.

claim: A total of 24 sampling sites were included, covering sampling periods of up to 31 years.
source: A total of 24 sampling sites were included, covering sampling periods of up to 31 years and representing four land use types of varying degrees of anthropogenic disturbance (Figure 1).
evidence: The methods section describes the spatial and temporal scope of the study and references a figure.

claim: ESB samples are collected and processed according to a highly standardized protocol at the same time every year.
source: ESB samples are collected and processed according to a highly standardized protocol at the same time every year.
evidence: The methods section describes the standardization of sample collection.

claim: Sampling events between different years of the time series usually do not differ by more than 2 weeks.
source: Sampling events between different years of the time series usually do not differ by more than 2 weeks.
evidence: The methods section describes the temporal consistency of sampling.

claim: All used equipment is sterilized before field work by several washes and heat treatments.
source: All used equipment is sterilized before field work by several washes and heat treatments (Tarricone et al., 2018a; Tarricone et al., 2018b; Klein et al., 2018).
evidence: The methods section describes the sterilization protocol and cites relevant studies.

claim: A defined amount of leaf material (>1.100 g) is collected from a defined number of trees (15 at most sites) from each site.
source: A defined amount of leaf material (>1.100 g) is collected from a defined number of trees (15 at most sites) from each site and from 4 branches from each tree.
evidence: The methods section describes the sampling protocol.

claim: The amount sampled translates to several thousand leaves from each site, which should suffice to saturate the recovered arthropod diversity.
source: The amount sampled translates to several thousand leaves from each site, which should suffice to saturate the recovered arthropod diversity.
evidence: The methods section explains the rationale for the sampling amount.

claim: The sampled leaves are intended to represent the exact natural state of the tree and are not washed or altered in any way before processing.
source: The sampled leaves are intended to represent the exact natural state of the tree. They are not washed or altered in any way before processing, and eDNA traces, and small arthropods on the leaves' surfaces, as well as from galls and leaf mines, are included in the sample.
evidence: The methods section describes the sample processing approach.

claim: Each sample is stored on liquid nitrogen immediately after collection and ground to a powder with an average diameter of 200 µm using a cryomill.
source: Each sample is stored on liquid nitrogen immediately after collection and ground to a powder with an average diameter of 200 µm using a cryomill.
evidence: The methods section describes the sample processing and storage.

claim: The cryomill is thoroughly cleaned between samples to prevent cross-contamination.
source: The cryomill is thoroughly cleaned between samples to prevent cross-contamination.
evidence: The methods section describes the contamination prevention measures.

claim: The resulting homogenates are stored for long term on liquid nitrogen.
source: The resulting homogenates are then stored for long term on liquid nitrogen (Rüdel et al., 2009; Rüdel et al., 2015).
evidence: The methods section describes the long-term storage and cites relevant studies.

claim: The cold chain is not interrupted after collection and during processing, ensuring optimal preservation of nucleic acids in the samples.
source: The cold chain is not interrupted after collection and during processing, ensuring optimal preservation of nucleic acids in the samples.
evidence: The methods section describes the preservation protocol.

claim: The homogenization of the sample guarantees a thorough mixing, resulting in equal distribution of environmental chemicals and probably eDNA in the sample.
source: The homogenization of the sample also guarantees a thorough mixing, resulting in equal distribution of environmental chemicals and probably eDNA in the sample.
evidence: The methods section explains the benefit of homogenization.

claim: Previous work suggests that very small subsamples of the homogenate suffice to detect even trace amounts of environmental chemicals in the sample.
source: Previous work suggests that very small subsamples of the homogenate suffice to detect even trace amounts of environmental chemicals in the sample (Gámez-Virués et al., 2015).
evidence: The methods section cites a study supporting the homogeneity of the samples.

claim: eDNA from leaf surfaces may be affected by weather conditions before sampling, for example, washed away by heavy rain or damaged by strong UV exposure.
source: eDNA from leaf surfaces may be affected by weather conditions before sampling, for example, washed away by heavy rain or damaged by strong UV exposure (Valentin et al., 2020).
evidence: The methods section cites a study about potential effects of weather on eDNA.

claim: Leaves are only collected dry by the ESB, that is, not immediately after rain.
source: However, leaves are only collected dry by the ESB, that is, not immediately after rain.
evidence: The methods section describes the sampling protocol to minimize weather effects.

claim: The date of the most recent rainfall is noted for each ESB sampling event.
source: The date of the most recent rainfall is noted for each ESB sampling event, allowing us to explore the effects of recent weather conditions on the recovered arthropod communities.
evidence: The methods section describes the metadata collected to assess weather effects.

claim: 200 mg of homogenate suffices to accurately recover α- and β-diversity.
source: This analysis confirms the pronounced homogenization of the samples, with 200 mg of homogenate sufficing to accurately recover α- and β-diversity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The methods section reports the validation of the extraction amount and references a figure.

claim: The primer pair ZBJ-ArtF1c/ZBJ-ArtR2c offers an ideal tradeoff between suppressing plant amplification while still recovering a taxonomically broad arthropod community.
source: We found an ideal tradeoff between suppressing plant amplification while still recovering a taxonomically broad arthropod community in the primer pair ZBJ-ArtF1c/ZBJ-ArtR2c (Zeale et al., 2011).
evidence: The methods section describes the primer selection and cites the original study.

claim: The ZBJ-ArtF1c/ZBJ-ArtR2c primer pair is known to have taxonomic biases for certain arthropod groups.
source: While this primer pair is known to have taxonomic biases for certain arthropod groups (Piñol et al., 2015), it is still widely used as an efficient and reliable marker for community analysis (Thomsen and Sigsgaard, 2019; Eitzinger et al., 2021).
evidence: The methods section acknowledges primer limitations and cites relevant studies.

claim: PCR and extraction replicates recovered a significantly lower β-diversity than within- and between-site comparisons.
source: PCR and extraction replicates also recovered a significantly lower β-diversity than within- and between-site comparisons (βPCR1vs2 = 0.14; βextract1vs2 = 0.19; βwithin site = 0.62; Pairwise Wilcoxon Test, p < 0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The methods section reports the validation of replication and references a figure.

claim: Patterns of diversity were highly correlated between duplicate and triplicate datasets (R2 = 0.95).
source: Patterns of diversity were highly correlated between duplicate and triplicate datasets (R2 = 0.95).
evidence: The methods section reports the validation of using duplicate PCRs.

claim: No signal of carryover was observed in the cryomill contamination test.
source: To ensure even minor carryover would be detected, we sequenced all samples to a high depth of 78,000 reads on average. Yet, no signal of carryover was observed (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The methods section reports the results of the contamination test.

claim: Arthropod DNA copy number showed negative associations with time (p < 0.001) and winter temperatures (p = 0.038).
source: Arthropod DNA copy number (marginal R2 = 0.26) showed negative associations with time (p < 0.001) and winter temperatures (p = 0.038).
evidence: The methods section reports the statistical analysis results for copy number.

claim: All richness values were positively correlated to winter temperatures and negatively to summer temperatures (marginal R2 = 0.45–0.48, p < 0.05).
source: However, all richness values were positively correlated to winter temperatures and negatively to summer temperatures (marginal R2 = 0.45–0.48, p < 0.05).
evidence: The methods section reports the statistical analysis results for richness.

claim: Genetic diversity (marginal R2 = 0.34) was correlated to winter rainfall (p < 0.001).
source: Genetic diversity (marginal R2 = 0.34) was correlated to winter rainfall (p < 0.001).
evidence: The methods section reports the statistical analysis results for genetic diversity.

claim: Gas chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry analysis shows that the detected pesticide load distinguishes the different land use types, with agricultural sites continuously showing the highest number of pesticides.
source: Gas chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (GC–MS/MS) analysis (Löbbert et al., 2021) shows that the detected pesticide load distinguishes the different land use types, with agricultural sites continuously showing the highest number of pesticides.
evidence: Figure 1 caption describes the pesticide analysis results and cites a relevant study.
